conceptTag: Equilibrium: when nobody wants to move
readerTitle: Why the smaller side of town can be the right place to stay
caseNote: 가상 사례 (창문 청소업체, 상점가 소매점) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 개념 출처는 Nash(1950).
insight: 경쟁 구도를 볼 때는 '어디가 더 큰가'가 아니라 '상대가 지금 선택을 유지할 때 내가 혼자 움직이면 더 나아지는가'를 묻는다.
misconception: 더 큰 시장이나 더 잘 버는 쪽으로 옮기면 나도 더 벌 수 있다. 덜 버는 쪽에 머무는 회사는 판단을 잘못한 것이다.

sources.text: Nash, J. F. (1950). Equilibrium points in n-person games. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 36(1), 48–49.
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 창문 청소 계산: 북쪽 60건, 남쪽 40건. 둘 다 북쪽이면 30/30, 둘 다 남쪽이면 20/20, 나눠 가지면 40/60 또는 60/40. 남쪽 업체가 북쪽으로 옮기면 40→30으로 줄고, 북쪽 업체가 남쪽으로 옮기면 60→20으로 줄어 둘 다 움직이지 않음. 30/30에서는 한쪽이 남쪽으로 가면 40으로 늘고, 20/20에서는 북쪽으로 가면 60으로 늘어 불안정. 건당 이익이 같다는 가정.
일요일 영업 계산: 혼자 열면 이익 $2,000, 둘 다 열면 각각 −$500(인건비 반영), 닫으면 $0. 경쟁사가 열고 내가 닫은 상태에서 내가 열면 $0→−$500, 경쟁사가 닫으면 $2,000→$0이므로 안정 상태. 설명용 가정 수치.
Nash(1950) PNAS 논문 서지 정보(권·호·쪽수)를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why the smaller side of town can be the right place to stay
body: Two window cleaners share a town. The North side has 60 jobs a week. The South side has 40.
One cleaner works the South side, earns less, and never moves. It isn't laziness or fear. It's arithmetic, and the numbers say staying put is the smart call.

image.label: A town split in two, with one window cleaner's van on each side
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 미니어처 마을. 강을 기준으로 위쪽 'North 60 jobs'(집이 더 많음), 아래쪽 'South 40 jobs'. 각 구역에 창문 청소 밴 한 대씩. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Should you move to the bigger side?
body: You clean windows on the South side: 40 jobs a week. Your rival has the North: 60 jobs. If you both work the North, you'd split it, about 30 each. Every job earns roughly the same.
Your rival isn't going anywhere. What do you do?

options.text: Move North. That's where most of the work is
options.feedback: The North is bigger, but you'd share it. You'd drop from 40 jobs to about 30 and leave the South empty.

options.text: Stay South and keep it well served
options.feedback: You give up the dream of 60, but 40 is the most you can get while your rival stays North. The next card shows why.

options.text: Split your week between both sides
options.feedback: You'd win some North jobs, but you'd lose South jobs and add driving time. Unless North customers switch to you in large numbers, you end up below 40.

cards.title: All four ways the town can split.

breakdown.label: Both North
breakdown.detail: Either cleaner gains by moving South (40)

breakdown.label: Both South
breakdown.detail: Either cleaner gains by moving North (60)

cards.callout: Read each pair as *you / rival*, in jobs per week. Only the two highlighted splits hold.

cards.title: Equilibrium
body: An **equilibrium** is a set of choices where no one can do better by changing only their own choice, given what everyone else is doing. The mathematician John Nash described it in 1950, which is why it's often called a *Nash equilibrium*.
It doesn't mean fair, and it doesn't mean best for everyone. At 40 / 60 you earn less than your rival. It just means nobody wants to move.

image.label: Two vans parked, each with a 'stay' arrow pointing back at itself
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 남쪽 밴 위에 'Move North: 40 → 30', 북쪽 밴 위에 'Move South: 60 → 20' 말풍선. 두 밴 모두 제자리로 돌아오는 화살표. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The one-question test.
body: You can check any situation in three steps:
list: Freeze what your rival is doing.
Ask: *would I earn more if I alone changed?*
Ask the same question for your rival.
cards.callout: If both answers are no, you've found an equilibrium. If either is yes, someone will eventually move.
cards.softwareNote: Two small software companies in one market often split niches: one serves agencies, the other freelancers. Chasing the bigger niche can look smart until you realize you'd be splitting it.

cards.title: Two stable answers. History picks one.
body: The town has two equilibria: you South and rival North, or the reverse. Both are stable. Which one happens usually depends on who arrived first.
The cleaner who settled the North early keeps the 60 jobs. The late arrival does best by taking the South, not by fighting for the North.
So when there's more than one stable outcome, timing and early moves matter a lot.

cards.title: Stable today isn't stable forever.
body: An equilibrium holds only while the numbers behind it hold. A new housing estate on the South side could make it 70 jobs. Then the North cleaner wants to move, and the whole map shifts.
It also assumes your rival thinks clearly. Pride, bad guesses or a new owner can push people out of a stable position, at least for a while. Check the numbers again whenever the market changes.

cards.title: Now it's two shops on a high street.
body: Your rival hardware store opens on Sundays and clears about $2,000 profit that day. You stay closed.
If you both opened, Sunday shoppers would split and each store would lose about $500 after staff costs. A consultant says: "They make $2,000 on Sundays. You should open too."

options.text: Open on Sundays to compete head-on
options.feedback: Your rival stays open either way, so you'd go from $0 to about −$500. You'd also wipe out their profit, which invites a fight.

options.text: Stay closed and strengthen the days you do well
options.feedback: With your rival open, closed is your best move, and open is theirs. That's an equilibrium. Your effort pays more on other days.
Smaller losses than opening all day, but you'd still be splitting a day that pays only one store. It's worth testing only if mornings bring different shoppers.

cards.title: Before you move, ask what you'd earn if only you moved.
body: A bigger market is not a better one if you have to share it. An equilibrium is where every player is already doing their best, given what the others do.
**Try it today:** pick one place you compete, such as a product, a location or opening hours. Freeze your rival's choice and write down what you'd earn if you alone changed yours.
